item.title: Pope Leo's doctors say tests show he needs no further treatment for lung cancer
item.description: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo’s doctors say that final tissue and molecular tests have confirmed that his lung cancer was localized and that no further treatment is needed, the Vatican said in a statement Wednesday. Pope Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday, four days after having the lower lobe of his right lung removed. The surgery confirmed that Leo had lung adenocarcinoma , the most common type of lung cancer. The pope's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the tests on tissue removed during the pope's surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread. “A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors said.

item.title: Trump says 'closest we've been' to ending Ukraine war
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday he believed an end to Russia's war on Ukraine could be closer than ever, as he thanked Russia's Vladimir Putin for freeing a detained American. "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way — maybe now the closest we've been," Trump told reporters at the White House. Trump has made similar claims before, but several rounds of talks and a summit with Putin in Alaska last year have failed to end the Ukraine war as Moscow sticks to its maximalist demands.

item.title: US 8th Army chief stresses readiness for threats beyond Korean Peninsula: report
item.description: WASHINGTON — The commander of the U.S. Eighth Army in South Korea has said his troops must be prepared to respond to threats beyond the Korean Peninsula, stressing that it would be "irresponsible" to focus solely on threats facing the peninsula, according to a media report Wednesday. Lt. Gen. Joseph Hilbert made the remarks in an email interview with the South China Morning Post, underscoring the U.S. military's emphasis on strategic flexibility. Hilbert said it would be "irresponsible to focus myopically" on threats on the Korean Peninsula alone or to "suggest that we cannot do other things simply because we are in Korea," according to the report. "We view readiness as largely threat-agnostic. If we have a trained, ready force capable of executing the Army's assigned missions, we can apply that force against whatever threat is required," Hilbert was quoted as saying. "So, we train every day with our Korean allies against our principal threat, while also ensuring we remain available and ready for whatever the nation may require," he added. item.title: Nasdaq climbs over 1% as SpaceX, Super Micro improve AI sentiment
item.description: The tech-heavy Nasdaq led gains on Wednesday after quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer improved appetite for AI-linked stocks, while Netflix slipped as its forecast failed to impress investors. Elon Musk's rocket and space technology firm rose 9.8 percent after he said on Tuesday that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be "a good idea". SpaceX also posted its first profit as a public company. Tesla shares were up 3.5 percent. Super Micro jumped 10.3 percent to the top of the S&P 500 after the AI server maker forecast quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates, signaling that AI demand remained resilient. Peers HPE and Dell rose 2.2 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively. Investors drew comfort from the reports as concerns over the profitability of the AI buildout triggered a selloff in AI-linked stocks last week, with data center operator CoreWeave at the center of the storm. item.title: Websites go dark worldwide as AI exposes critical security flaws
item.description: WASHINGTON — Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites Wednesday after two critical flaws came to light involving PHP, a programming language that is the basis for a large share of the internet. PHP sits underneath popular web design platforms, so the weaknesses potentially affect a vast range of websites, from online stores and news outlets to government services. Wiz, one of the security firms that found the issues, estimated that PHP runs about 70 percent of the world's websites and said the flaws rank "among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history." The US National Security Agency told organizations to patch immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline. The flaws "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," the NSA said in a statement on X. Attackers could use them to take over web servers without needing a password. item.title: Nvidia adds Samsung Electro-Mechanics to substrate supply chain, plans capacity expansion in S. Korea
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. chip giant Nvidia Corp. said Wednesday that South Korea's Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co. is joining its semiconductor substrate supply chain as part of a broader initiative to expand manufacturing capacity. Samsung Electro-Mechanics, the electronic components unit of Samsung Electronics Co., will initially provide production capacity from its existing operations in South Korea, while the collaboration will also support facility upgrades and new factories in Sejong and Busan, South Korea, according to Nvidia. By 2028, production allocated to Nvidia is projected to account for a significant portion of Samsung Electro-Mechanics' total annual package substrate production capacity, the U.S. company said. The South Korean company also issued a separate press release, calling the deal a strategic business partnership to strengthen the global artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor supply chain. Samsung Electro-Mechanics said it plans to supply Nvidia with package substrates for AI semiconductors under a multiyear agreement beginning in 2026. Separately, Nvidia and U.S.-base

item.title: What is PHP and why did it take government websites offline?
item.description: Government websites across Europe went dark on Wednesday as operators raced to patch two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the most widely used programming languages on the web. The developers of PHP said on Wednesday they would release patches for two critical vulnerabilities, and EU cybersecurity officials warned organisations unable to apply the fixes to take affected websites offline. Here is what you need to know: What is PHP? PHP is a programming language that runs websites. It works behind the scenes. When a user loads a page, the server running PHP assembles the content and sends the finished page to the browser. It is free, open source and maintained by volunteers. Site owners rarely interact with it directly. PHP runs nearly 70 percent of all websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs. It is the engine behind WordPress, the software that powers about 40 percent of all websites such as blogs, small business pages, government portals, online shops and news sites. item.title: Putin agrees to resume 3-way talks with Kyiv and Washington
item.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, a Kremlin official said. The Russian leader has agreed “in principle” to resume the talks after Nov. 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters following a meeting in St. Petersburg between Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff. The talks will focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends,” Ushakov said. Witkoff's talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as Trump pushed Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that only a summit of leaders can break the impasse. The two armies remain locked on the battlefield, and the two countries pummel each other with daily long-range strikes. Representatives of the three countries held three rounds of negotiations early this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva

item.title: Netanyahu says 'toppling' Iran government only way to end threat
item.description: DIMONA, Israel — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that the only way to remove the threat posed by Iran was to topple its government. "Iran wanted to destroy us; we stopped them. They wanted to produce nuclear bombs; we stopped them... Yet they persist," he said during an election rally in the southern town of Dimona. "Therefore, there is only one way to end this: by toppling this regime." "This is the directive I have issued to the Israel Defense Forces, to the Mossad, and to all our security branches," he added, without specifying when or how that directive would be executed. The sabre-rattling came as the premier headed into the last week of a tight race for re-election. Netanyahu had instructed the Israeli military to plan for resumed strikes against Iran earlier this month, according to sources cited by the Financial Times on Wednesday, but US President Donald Trump reportedly objected to the idea. item.title: France's Macron vows order, calls foreign criticism of unrest 'stupid'
item.description: PARIS — President Emmanuel Macron vowed on Wednesday to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence at protests planned in the coming days, and dismissed as "stupid" and "unacceptable" comments from some foreign leaders about the unrest. France's main student union, UNEF, has called for further rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest group, which emerged as a potent anti-establishment movement in 2018, has filed plans for a march through central Paris the same day. Efforts to ease social tensions showed little sign of progress, as unions pledged to press ahead with a general strike on November 5 to denounce the high cost of living and cuts to public services after government talks ended inconclusively. France was hit by some of the worst urban tumult in years on October 17 on the fringe of nationwide protests, shocking the nation both because of its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it. Macron said he would meet intelligence officials and senior ministers on Thursday to discuss the crisis. "Those who want to cause disorder in city centres next Saturday will be pre

item.title: OpenAI says its AI agents disabled their own safety monitors
item.description: WASHINGTON — OpenAI has revealed that two of its artificial intelligence agents disabled or weakened systems built to catch them misbehaving, with one later denying it had done so. The cases are the latest in a string of safety scares at the world's top AI developers involving agents, AI programs that carry out tasks without human involvement. In a report released Tuesday, the ChatGPT maker said that during two internal coding jobs, its agents switched off or undermined tools for detecting incidents of AI models acting against human wishes. On October 3, an agent running on OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol model, which had been told not to send any messages on the workplace chat app, took that as license to switch off safety alerts meant for the company's security team while fixing a testing system. Three days later, a GPT-6 Astra agent stripped out its own monitor while copying code from another project, then told the human programmer it had done no such thing. The company said it had also seen several cases of agents launching software with monitoring switched off, exposing a gap in its oversight

item.title: Lee meets with WHO chief to discuss cooperation in healthcare
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung met with World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus on Wednesday to discuss ways to enhance cooperation in healthcare, Lee's office said. The meeting at Cheong Wa Dae came as Tedros is visiting Seoul to attend the World Bio Summit 2026, which WHO is hosting in partnership with South Korea on Wednesday and Thursday. During the meeting, Lee stressed the need for South Korea to expand its role and contributions to the international community, presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan said in a written briefing. Lee also expressed hope that Seoul would continue to expand its cooperation with WHO in health security. The president asked Tedros to help ensure that more highly skilled South Koreans could contribute to the WHO, noting that South Korea has transformed itself from a recipient of international assistance into a major contributor. Tedros thanked South Korea for its efforts to strengthen cooperation with WHO and promote global health, saying he was well aware of the country's development experience. item.title: 'No retirement from giving': Catholic priest returns to school to care for elderly
item.description: A Catholic priest in his 60s who has spent his life serving others is embarking on a new educational journey after decades away from the classroom, hoping to continue his service to the elderly after retirement. Father Carlo Yoon Haeng-do, 65, is head of the Wolyeong Catholic Church in the Diocese of Masan. Yoon enrolled in a master's program in social welfare at Kyungnam University in South Gyeongsang Province in March. He returned to his studies after nearly 30 years to prepare for a new chapter of service to the elderly after retirement. Although priests step down from active ministry at 70, Yoon believes that “there is no retirement from serving one's neighbors.” “As the elderly population grows, someone has to work for older people, and older people themselves should also take part in that work,” he said with a broad smile. Yoon begins each day by rising around 3 a.m. and praying for about two hours before cleaning the church and nearby alleyways. item.title: "A Spark from the Cockroaches": Arundhati Roy on India's Youth Protests & Modi's Crackdown
item.description:
A court in India on Wednesday ordered the release of two leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, the youth-led movement that has led historic waves of protests in India since the summer. Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were detained amid massive protests last week after they scaled a barricade to enter a site popular for protest, unfurled the national flag and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Kumar oversaw the deletion of 130 million names from the voter rolls in India since June of last year. Opposition parties say those impacted are primarily Muslims and other minorities less likely to support the BJP, the Hindu nationalist ruling party of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

“You have a deep and wide — an ideologically wide — historical culture of resistance in India,” says acclaimed writer and activist Arundhati Roy. At the same time, the Modi government “has three things in its playbook: One is false-flag attacks, two is engineering communal riots, and the third is massive repression. And I don’t think we’ve seen its hand yet.”

item.title: Should AIPAC Register as a Foreign Agent? Zeteo Examines Pro-Israel Lobby's Influence on Elections
item.description:
The growing controversy over AIPAC’s impact on U.S. politics is the subject of a new Zeteo documentary titled Night Flower: Inside AIPAC’s Fight for Influence. The film examines AIPAC’s history and its role in shaping U.S. policy toward Israel, and questions whether its activities warrant further scrutiny under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, or FARA. “It says that you have to register under this law if you are acting at the request of a foreign government,” says Dion Nissenbaum, the filmmaker behind Night Flower: Inside AIPAC’s Fight for Influence. “And we talked to numerous people who showed us several examples of how AIPAC is acting at the request of Israel.”

Referencing the title of the film, Night Flower, Zeteo editor-in-chief Mehdi Hasan says AIPAC “blossoms in the dark, shrivels in the light. We’re trying to put some sunlight onto AIPAC.”

item.title: Mehdi Hasan on AIPAC's Role in El-Sayed vs. Rogers Race in Michigan & Trump's Targeting of Ilhan Omar
item.source:markdown:
One of the most closely watched races in the midterm elections is in Michigan between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed is a former public health official who is campaigning on a platform of Medicare for All, ending military aid to Israel, and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers is a former Republican congressman backed by President Trump.
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate. During Wednesday’s debate in Michigan, Rogers repeated the claim, without providing evidence, that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied the accusation.
“If Abdul El-Sayed wins, it will be a reminder that the left can win in a swing state like Michigan,” says Mehdi Hasan, editor-in-chief of _Zeteo_. “And it will be actually a moment to say, 'You know what? Americans rejected Islamophobia.'”

item.title: Police seek arrest warrant for man over Seoul arson attacks that injured 19
item.description: Police said Wednesday they have sought a formal arrest warrant for a man on suspicion of arson resulting in injury after he set fires at two buildings in southern Seoul earlier this week, leaving 19 people injured. The suspect was taken into custody hours after setting fires at separate patent firms housed in the two buildings in Seoul's Gangnam district Tuesday. The incident left 19 people injured, including one who was rushed to a hospital in cardiac arrest. The suspect told investigators that he bought two jerrycans, a lighter and flammable material near his home in western Seoul on Friday, according to the police. He claimed the patent firms had defrauded him by issuing fake patent registration certificates, and that he had wanted to scare them and let the world know, the police said.

item.title: France's tourism sector worried about impact of riots
item.description: PARIS — The images of France's riots posted and broadcast around the world have cast a pall on the country's important tourism sector, with many fearing worse consequences if violence returns. "The surge of violence in the centers of Nice, Paris, Lyon — it's catastrophic," said Christelle Cassagne, head of the ADN Tourisme body covering the country's tourism institutions. "When you book a hotel for a week, it's not so you stay stuck in the hotel," she said. The scenes of clashes with police, public buildings on fire, shops being looted and masked young men roaming the streets have, since last weekend, shocked and fascinated news audiences internationally. The violence has usurped the usual curated footage of genteel cafes favored by influencers, who have suddenly taken to asking "Is Paris safe?" — many using AI on thumbnails or even in their videos to boost click-through rates. Even in Paris, some tourists who had front-row seats to the convulsion on the streets are looking for the exit. And others coming in were hesitant. item.title: National museum chief resigns over misattributed work from private collection
item.description: You Hong-june, director of the National Museum of Korea, resigned Wednesday amid a controversy over the museum's display of a misattributed calligraphic work from his private collection. He offered to resign earlier in the day, and President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation. You came under fire after the piece, written by a prominent pro-Japanese collaborator during Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule of Korea, was wrongly introduced as the work of a Korean independence activist and was found to be from his private collection. The museum removed the item from its ongoing special exhibition following the controversy. In a statement sent to reporters, You said he has concluded that he should step down "to restore the museum's tarnished honor." "The deep trust the public has placed in the National Museum of Korea and the value our staff has built collapsed in an instant because of my personal mistake," he said. "All criticism over this matter is entirely my responsibility." You, a prominent art historian and author of the bestselling book series "My Exploration of Cultural Heritage," apologiz

item.title: N. Korea to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts toward S. Korea: Kim Yo-jong
item.description: Kim Yo-jong, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un's sister, said Wednesday that Pyongyang will resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts toward South Korea later this month, state media reported. "Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border," Kim said in a statement carried in an English-language dispatch by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). ROK stands for the Republic of Korea, South Korea's official name. Kim, a department director at the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, described the move as the "most just measure" and an "appropriate response." She said she inspected key positions along the southern border earlier in the day with Pak Jong-chon, an adviser to the North's Ministry of National Defense, to review progress on a project to fortify the border. Kim corrected an earlier KCNA report that had said the inspection took place Tuesday. "Our army is carrying out a crucial and great undertaking in the face of the enemy's persistent threats

item.title: Cold wave advisory set to take effect Thursday night as temperatures drop 10 degrees
item.description: Thursday morning temperatures are forecast to drop about 10 degrees Celsius from Wednesday, with parts of northeastern Gyeonggi Province and inland and mountainous Gangwon Province dipping below freezing. A cold wave advisory will take effect after midnight Thursday for most inland areas. It is issued from October to April when the morning low is forecast to fall at least 10 degrees from the previous day to 3 degrees or below and to run at least 3 degrees below normal. Morning lows on Thursday are forecast at 0 to 10 degrees nationwide. Frost will form in inland areas and ice in eastern Gyeonggi Province, inland and mountainous Gangwon Province, North Chungcheong Provice, northeastern North Jeolla Province and inland central and northeastern mountainous areas of North Gyeongsang Province. Daytime highs will stay between 14 and 19 degrees. Temperatures will swing by 15 degrees or more between morning and afternoon. item.title: Busan authorities guide shark out of canal on third attempt
item.description: Authorities in the southeastern port city of Busan successfully guided a shark out of a city canal Wednesday on their third attempt after the animal spent more than a month trapped there. The shark — named "Bukangi" after Bukhang, the Korean word for North Port — was first spotted in the canal Sept. 18. Since then, the canal park has turned into a major attraction, drawing over 1.6 million visitors as of Sunday. A joint rescue team involving municipal and Coast Guard officials used a net secured to a flat floating platform to drive the shark out of the canal at Busan's North Port, located about 330 kilometers southeast of Seoul. Authorities began the operation around 10 a.m., steering the shark toward Marina Bridge with the net. The shark, which had been swimming near the bridge, was spotted in waters outside the canal near a pier at around 6 p.m. The sighting indicated that Bukangi had left the canal, at least for the time being. However, the waters near the pier are not considered open sea. Authorities hope the shark will eventually make its way to open waters. After two previous att

item.title: [VIDEO] Beyond the cup: Korea's evolving cafe industry
item.description: Korea is home to roughly 100,000 cafes. How did the coffee industry thrive to this extent in a country that is not historically known for coffee? Looking at Mega MGC Coffee — the chain with the largest number of branches in Korea — two key factors emerge. On average, a Korean consumes nearly 400 cups of coffee per year, which is almost three times the global average. For Koreans, coffee is less of a leisurely break and more of a functional "potion" used to endure demanding workloads. Because of this, cafes in Korea generally adopt one of two distinct strategies: they either position themselves as high-end establishments, or they brand themselves as low-cost options to maximize profit through high sales volume rather than high margins per drink. Mega MGC Coffee falls into the latter category. By pricing an iced Americano at around 2,000 won($1.5) for a 710ml cup, the company focuses on becoming part of the daily routine for consumers rather than making a large profit from each sale. item.title: Top US envoy cites 'turbulence' in S. Korea-US alliance amid rift in security, trade priorities
item.description: The top U.S. envoy to South Korea on Wednesday described bilateral relations between Seoul and Washington as being in a state of "turbulence," stressing efforts to move the alliance forward into a stronger and more equal partnership. U.S. Ambassador Michelle Steel's remarks come amid apparent friction in the security and trade ties, from implementing their summit agreement from last October and intelligence sharing on North Korea to Seoul's push to retake wartime operational control (OPCON) from Washington. "This is, kind of, like a turbulence that we are going through between the Republic of Korea and the U.S.," she said during a dialogue session hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea (AMCHAM), referring to South Korea by its official name. "An alliance does not mean it stays always the same. It can be weaker, and we can move forward to be stronger. This is exactly what we are working on," she said. Seoul and Washington have agreed on a series of economic and security commitments, including nuclear energy, shipbuilding cooperation and South Korean investment in the U.S., fo

item.title: Lee Sun-bin embraces comedy, chaos in movie about college entrance exam
item.description: In the upcoming comedy film "Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng," actor Lee Sun-bin plays Maeng Bo-ram, an earnest provincial high school teacher who unexpectedly finds herself locked away in a top-secret camp to draft questions for the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT). Ahead of the movie's theatrical release, Lee expressed both anxiety and anticipation during a recent interview in Seoul, saying the unique subject of the annual exam posed its own challenges. "This moment right before the release is both the time I want to avoid and the moment I look forward to," Lee told The Korea Times at a cafe in Seoul on Wednesday. "I tend to be harsh on myself and worry about my shortcomings. At the same time, I am deeply curious whether audiences will recognize actors’ intentions behind the performance. It feels like I am scared, but also eager to face the verdict as soon as possible." The movie centers on the 40-day isolation period where test developers are completely cut off from the outside world under strict security. item.title: K-pop soars on Asian tour revenue, physical album sales
item.description: K-pop is riding a surge in concert ticket and physical album sales, two of the industry's key revenue streams, as data released this month showed the genre dominating Asia's touring market and closing in on 100 million album sales for the year. The two businesses sit at the core of K-pop agencies' earnings. At HYBE, concerts brought in 647.7 billion won ($488.5 million) of its record 1.45 trillion won in second-quarter revenue, while albums and digital music accounted for 326.8 billion won, followed closely by merchandise and licensing at 310.6 billion won. K-pop acts took six of the 10 highest-grossing touring spots in Asia over the past year, led by boy band Seventeen, which grossed $97.4 million and sold 661,088 tickets, according to U.S. concert industry publication Pollstar's Asia Focus Top Touring Artists chart. The chart covers shows played between Aug. 1, 2025, and July 31, 2026. K-pop acts filled the chart's top four spots. TWICE came in second with $76.18 million, followed by TXT and BTS, which grossed $49.07 million in Asia as part of its "ARIRANG" world tour. BLACKPINK and EN

item.title: Prosecutors seek 5-year prison term for pastor over courthouse riot
item.description: Prosecutors on Wednesday requested a five-year prison term for conservative activist pastor Jeon Kwang-hoon over his alleged involvement in a courthouse riot last year by supporters of former President Yoon Suk Yeol. The Seoul Western District Prosecutors Office sought the sentence during a hearing at the Seoul Western District Court, where Jeon faced multiple charges, including instigating trespassing in special-protection buildings. Jeon is accused of being behind pro-Yoon protesters' violence at the same court on Jan. 19 last year, following the court's decision to extend Yoon's detention over his martial law declaration in December 2024. The prosecution also charged Jeon with violating the Assembly and Demonstration Act and obstructing general traffic for urging rally participants gathered in Gwanghwamun Square to march toward the court one day before the violence. The prosecution also charged Jeon with violating the Assembly and Demonstration Act and obstructing general traffic for urging rally participants gathered in Gwanghwamun Square to march toward the court one day before the violence. item.title: IVE turns Seoul's futuristic DDP into K-pop comeback stage
item.description: Seoul is transforming one of its most iconic architectural landmarks into a high-octane venue for K-pop, partnering with girl group IVE to launch its latest comeback campaign at Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) in an effort to turn global fandom into tourism revenues and longer hotel stays. The Seoul Metropolitan Government and Seoul Design Foundation are supporting the campaign, titled “DIVE IN TO LIGHT,” which began Monday at DDP and runs through Nov. 30. The building’s exterior displays special videos featuring IVE, with a more elaborate presentation planned to coincide with the release of the group’s new album on Monday, when synchronized laser effects and lighting will accompany its new music. A promotional booth is operating at DDP from 5:30 p.m. to 11 p.m. through Nov. 1, featuring album-themed photo zones and displays of hero masks worn by IVE members. item.title: Gwanghwamun memorial garden draws 500,000 visitors, celebrates Swedish ties
item.description: Seoul’s Garden of Gratitude has drawn more than 500,000 visitors in its first 160 days, as the memorial space prepares to celebrate its ties with Sweden through a weekend of cultural events, performances and a special light display. The Seoul Metropolitan Government said the garden recorded 500,157 visitors as of Monday, according to an automated counting system. Located at Gwanghwamun Square, the garden honors countries and veterans who fought in the 1950-53 Korean War and invites visitors to reflect on freedom, peace and international solidarity. Its outdoor installation, “23 Lights of Gratitude,” symbolizes appreciation for the countries that supported Korea during the war, while an underground exhibition hall called Freedom Hall uses digital media to tell the story of the conflict and Korea’s transformation from an aid recipient into a donor nation. Sweden has added a new element to the memorial, donating syenite quarried in Ekeröd, Sweden, in August, the city said. item.description: Seoul will turn meditation, traditional cuisine and live music into a citywide invitation to slow down as it hosts Seoul Wellness Travel Week beginning Saturday, with programs centered on Gangnam District and eight wellness destinations across the city. Organized by the Seoul Metropolitan Government, the 12-day event, running until Nov. 4, will showcase experiences designed around three themes: rest, food and culture, under the slogan “Seoul, Defines the Next Wellness.” At Bongeunsa Temple, visitors can join sound-bowl meditation, yoga, tea gatherings and restorative exercise on Saturday and Sunday, with 15 wellness programs planned across the two days. Highlights include a meditation session led by Ven. Geumgang, chair of the Jogye Order’s Seon Meditation Committee, and an evening walking meditation through the temple grounds. Most temple programs cost 5,000 won ($3.60), while Ven. Geumgang’s meditation session is free. item.title: Trump and Republicans blame France's immigrants for riots without evidence
item.description: PARIS — U.S. President Donald Trump and leading Republicans are trying to leverage widespread riots in France ahead of midterm congressional elections by making unsubstantiated claims that the social unrest in Europe is caused by Muslim migrants. Peaceful nationwide demonstrations in France over the high cost of living and in support of students' grievances over underfunded schools turned violent over the weekend, with masked rioters committing vandalism and clashing with overwhelmed police. In Italy’s finance and fashion capital of Milan on Saturday, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Here's a closer look at the facts. CLAIM: Migrants of Muslim heritage are doing most of the damage in France and Italy. THE FACTS: It is difficult to know the exact sociological makeup of the protesters, but no one group has been singled out as being responsible for the violence. item.title: Korean won extends gains against US dollar on strong exports
item.description: The Korean won extended its gains to hit a fresh two-year high against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, supported by strong exports and foreign inflows. The won was quoted at 1,325.2 won per dollar at 3:30 p.m., up 2.9 won from the close of the previous stock trading session. For a fourth straight session, the won marked the highest level since Oct. 2, 2024. Earlier in the day, government data showed that the nation's exports more than doubled to US$61.6 billion in the first 20 days of October, driven by robust shipments of semiconductor. Foreign purchased a net 659.9 billion won ($497.3 million) worth of local shares during the latest regular stock trading session, with the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index gaining 3.29 percent to close at 5,735.66.

item.description: The Korean Peninsula faces a rapidly evolving threat environment, U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) Commander Gen. Xavier Brunson and a senior U.S. official said in back-to-back warnings from Seoul and Washington, raising questions about how those changes could affect the timing of the transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON). Their remarks followed a renewed dispute over the OPCON transfer after Brunson suggested on Oct. 14 that evolving threats called for new transition standards, drawing objections from Seoul’s defense ministry and an unusual response from President Lee Jae Myung. “Our security environment is not standing still. item.title: Lee says AI should be used to bridge health care gaps worldwide
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung said Wednesday that artificial intelligence (AI) technology should be used responsibly in the health care sector to bridge health care gaps worldwide. The president delivered the message in a speech to the World Bio Summit 2026 in Seoul, which was read on his behalf by his senior secretary for social affairs, Kim Kyoung-ja. The World Health Organization is hosting the event Wednesday and Thursday in collaboration with the Korean government. "In the health care sector, which is directly connected to human lives, AI technology should be used safely and responsibly to bridge gaps in medical services worldwide," the president said. The summit adopted the "AI Healthcare Seoul Declaration," calling for global solidarity to ensure that the benefits from AI innovations are shared by all and that AI technology is used in safe and responsible manners. "Narrowing gaps between countries in the health care sector and ensuring that everyone has access to proper medical services is the task of our time, and everyone should work together to accomplish it," Lee noted.

item.title: Seoul eyes long-term digital infrastructure projects via sovereign wealth fund
item.description: SEJONG — Korea plans to provide patient capital for long-term digital infrastructure projects through the country's planned sovereign wealth fund, the second vice finance minister has said. Second Vice Finance Minister Huh Chang outlined the plan during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Finance Ministers' Meeting held in Hong Kong from Tuesday to Wednesday, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy. Huh's remarks came after Korea unveiled plans earlier this year to launch a new sovereign wealth fund in 2027 to make continuous investments in cutting-edge and strategic industries. item.title: Mercedes-Benz Korea promotes safer driving with Beyond Driving campaign
item.description: Mercedes-Benz Korea is expanding its road safety efforts, drawing on its automotive expertise and safety experience to promote more considerate driving. The company’s Corporate Social Responsibility Committee recently launched Beyond Driving, a campaign that encourages motorists to adopt safer everyday driving habits, extending its safety initiatives beyond children to drivers of all ages. The committee has promoted road safety in Korea for over a decade, starting with MobileKids, a traffic safety education program for children in 2014. Its initiatives have since expanded to include school-zone safety campaigns, online and in-person education programs and radio campaigns, collectively reaching more than 50,000 children. This year, the committee broadened its focus to drivers nationwide with Beyond Driving, emphasizing that safer roads depend not only on compliance with traffic laws but also on drivers being considerate of one another and yielding when necessary. The inspection came after the South Korean military vowed Tuesday to take "decisive" action if the North stages further provocations, following Pyongyang's threat to deploy strike means along the border. item.title: Samsung Biologics Q3 net income down over 20%
item.description: Samsung Biologics, the biotech arm of Samsung Group, on Wednesday reported its third-quarter net profit of 391.1 billion won ($295.2 million), down 21.2 percent from a year earlier. The contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) service provider, which offers comprehensive development and manufacturing solutions, said in a regulatory filing that it posted 640.1 billion won in operating profit for the quarter, compared with 633.5 billion won a year ago. Revenue rose 18.5 percent to 1.49 trillion won. The company attributed its sales increase to full-scale operations at four plants in Songdo, just west of Seoul, a ramp-up in production at its fifth plant, as well as sales generated from its first U.S.-based biomanufacturing facility in Rockville, Maryland, acquired in March. item.description: Actor Eum Moon-suk is set to get married in January. A representative of his agency, Ghost Studio, told Hankook Ilbo on Wednesday that Eum “will marry his girlfriend in January next year.” According to reports, his fiancée currently works as a model, and the couple will tie the knot after dating for a long time. Born in 1982, Eum made his debut as a singer in 2005 and appeared on Mnet’s dance competition program “Dancing 9” in 2013. item.title: Gangnam arson attack renews alarm over elderly men with grudges
item.description: A man in his 70s arrested on suspicion of injuring 19 people in an arson attack cited a personal grudge as his motive, renewing concern over elderly people driven by resentment starting fires. On Tuesday, two buildings in Seoul’s Gangnam District were set on fire and the suspect was caught fleeing. He mostly acknowledged planning and committing the arson, police said Wednesday. He is believed to have harbored a grievance against patent law firms over their handling of a trademark registration. When reporters asked about his motive, he shouted that the firms had cheated him. Asked what he would say to the victims, he replied, “Tell them to stop cheating people.” The suspect had already been detained in 2022 for preparing to commit arson after visiting the same two law firms, dousing employees with gasoline and threatening them with a lighter. The case is the latest in a pattern of arson attacks by older adults acting on accumulated grudges. item.title: Korea's crypto tax faces 4th delay as gov't turns cautious amid low approval ratings
item.description: Korea’s tax on cryptocurrency gains, scheduled to take effect in January, could face a fourth postponement as the government turns cautious amid mounting calls for a delay from investors, the industry and lawmakers from both ruling and opposition parties. Authorities have defended the levy on the principle that income should be taxed and on grounds of fairness across asset classes. However, the government’s recent pledge to reassess tax infrastructure and market conditions has fueled expectations of another postponement. The subtle shift comes as falling stock prices and tighter property taxation have already frustrated investors, raising concerns that crypto taxation could provoke further backlash. Low approval ratings for President Lee Jae Myung and the ruling party are adding to the political pressure. The issue is particularly sensitive among young investors. Under the current timetable, the first filing and payment deadline would fall in May 2028, immediately after parliamentary elections that April. On Wednesday, Rep. item.title: Election official found dead after special counsel questioning
item.description: A National Election Commission (NEC) official was found dead Wednesday, a day after being questioned by a special counsel team investigating the election watchdog in connection with the unprecedented ballot shortages in the local elections. According to the sources, the official in his 40s was found in the flowerbed of an apartment building in Hwaseong, about 45 kilometers south of Seoul, at 7:06 a.m. with a suicide note expressing grievances he felt during the questioning. Police suspect he jumped from his apartment. The investigation team has been looking into why the ballot shortages happened and if any corruption or irregularities were involved in contracts for election-related supplies, such as early voting ballot boxes and voting site banners used in last year's presidential election and the June 3 local elections. The deceased underwent questioning at the investigation team's office Tuesday as a suspect over alleged obstruction of the bidding process and breach of trust. item.title: KB Life CEO joins campaign against illegal lending
item.description: KB Life Insurance CEO Jeong Mun-cheol has joined a nationwide campaign against illegal private lending, pledging to help protect the financially vulnerable and promote financial inclusion, the insurer said Wednesday. Launched in July by the Korea Inclusive Finance Agency, the “Finance That Saves Lives” campaign brings together financial institutions, government agencies and local governments. It follows a relay format, where participants share a message raising public awareness of inclusive finance and nominate the next person to carry it forward. The initiative aligns with the Lee Jae Myung administration’s push for inclusive finance, which includes expanding access to financial services, easing the burden on delinquent borrowers and cracking down on illegal lending. Jeong was nominated by KB Kookmin Bank CEO Lee Hwan-ju on Sept. 28. item.title: Appeals court slashes ex-justice minister's sentence to 9 years over martial law role
item.description: An appellate court on Wednesday significantly reduced former Justice Minister Park Sung-jae's sentence from 25 years to nine years in prison over his role in former President Yoon Suk Yeol's failed martial law bid. The Seoul High Court handed down the lighter sentence, convicting Park of playing a key role in an insurrection under Yoon's short-lived declaration of martial law in December 2024, while overturning a lower court's conviction on multiple other charges. The appellate court ruled Park was aware that Yoon's emergency decree did not meet the substantive and procedural conditions for martial law, and the declaration was made for unconstitutional and illegal purposes. item.description: An appellate court on Wednesday handed down suspended prison terms for three former officials for forcibly repatriating two North Korean fishermen in 2019 despite their intention to defect to South Korea. The Seoul High Court upheld a lower court's guilty verdicts for Chung Eui-yong, former national security adviser; former National Intelligence Service Director Suh Hoon; and former Unification Minister Kim Yeon-chul. It, however, acquitted former Presidential chief of staff Noh Young-min, who had earlier been convicted over his involvement in the case. All four served in former President Moon Jae-in's administration in November 2019, when Seoul deported two North Korean fishermen back to North Korea after they were captured near the eastern maritime border. The fishermen had been accused of killing 16 crew members. The move sparked outcry from critics as the fishermen had expressed their intent to defect to South Korea, which maintains a policy of accepting North Korean defectors. item.description: SEJONG — Korea's budget minister on Wednesday vowed to look into potential vulnerabilities in the country's funding for firefighters, amid concerns that they have become a financial burden for regional governments. "I agree that the issue needs to be carefully examined," Budget Minister Park Hong-geun said during a meeting with reporters in the central city of Sejong. "We have not yet held detailed internal discussions on how the situation should be improved," Park said. Choo Mi-ae recently described firefighters as a "fiscal drain," triggering public backlash while drawing attention to underlying issues in the funding system. item.description: Align Partners disclosed that it holds a 1.5 percent stake in SK Inc. through its fund, arguing that the holding company's share price does not fully reflect the value of its key subsidiary, SK hynix. According to materials presented by Align CEO Lee Chang-hwan at the "13D Monitor Active-Passive Investor Summit" in New York on Tuesday (local time), the activist fund held 1,088,753 shares of SK Inc., representing 1.5 percent of the holding company's total outstanding shares. Lee described SK Inc. as an opportunity to gain exposure to world-class artificial intelligence assets at a discounted valuation. SK Inc. holds a 32.2 percent stake in SK Square, which in turn owns about 20 percent of SK hynix. It gives SK Inc. an effective stake of roughly 6.5 percent in the chipmaker. He explained that the value of SK Inc.'s indirect stake in SK hynix is subject to two layers of discounts due to its ownership structure. item.title: DPK considering parliamentary probe into Supreme Court chief amid impeachment calls
item.description: The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) said Wednesday it is considering launching a parliamentary investigation into Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae amid an ongoing debate within the party over whether to seek his impeachment. Following a meeting of the party's supreme council, DPK spokesperson Cho Gye-won told reporters that the party was considering launching such a probe to look into "specific grounds" for impeaching the chief justice after the ongoing parliamentary audit ends later this month. When asked whether the probe would be aimed at impeaching the chief justice, the lawmaker replied, "It is intended to shed light on the grounds for impeachment ... so it could be seen that way." The announcement came after DPK leader Kim Min-seok said on Friday that the party has begun discussing various options to impeach Cho. item.title: [COVER STORY] French residents of Korea blame unresponsive gov't for unrest
item.description: The public anger in France spilling over into unrest has been brewing for a long time, with little response from the government over calls for reforms for better education and living conditions, French nationals living in Korea say. They generally agree that the French government's long-standing neglect and inaction have fueled mounting public anger, saying people's concerns have long gone unheard. "Government hasn’t listened enough to people’s concerns about the climate, the economy and now education. When people repeatedly feel unheard, frustration builds up," Hugo Adam, a graduate student at Seoul National University, told The Korea Times. A French filmmaker, who spoke on condition of anonymity, agreed that the French government has failed to "listen to its people," despite the many protests that have taken place over the years. He said his family and friends back home are participating in the protests. The protests began in mid-September by students calling for a better education environment, including more teachers and improved school facilities. Illustrator Zoe Constans said it

item.title: Seoul stocks rebound over 3% on eased AI spending woes
item.description: Korean stocks rebounded Wednesday, recovering from the previous session's steep losses as semiconductor shares rallied on easing concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending. The Korean won strengthened against the U.S. dollar. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) gained 182.92 points, or 3.29 percent, to close at 5,735.66 after rising as high as 5,816.43. The sharp rally prompted the Korea Exchange (KRX) to activate a buy-side sidecar shortly before 11 a.m., temporarily suspending program buying for five minutes after KOSPI 200 futures rose more than 5 percent. It marked the first such activation in two months. The rebound came after the main index plunged nearly 4 percent the previous session amid renewed concerns over massive AI infrastructure spending. Investor sentiment improved after better-than-expected earnings from U.S. AI server maker Super Micro Computer helped ease worries over AI-related investments, lifting shares of chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. item.title: Incheon locals oppose plan to move Overseas Koreans Agency to Sejong
item.description: Political parties, local officials and civic activists in Incheon are pushing back against the government’s plan to relocate the Overseas Koreans Agency (OKA) to Sejong, calling the decision unilateral and demanding it be scrapped. The Ministry of the Interior and Safety announced Oct. 13 that 44 ministries and agencies would relocate in phases beginning next year through 2031 as part of a national strategy to break up the capital area-centered administrative system. The agency, which oversees diaspora policy under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is among the first six agencies slated to move — scheduled to leave its Incheon headquarters for the administrative city of Sejong by the first half of 2027. The OKA was originally established in Incheon following fierce competition among local governments, with the city selected for its proximity to Incheon International Airport and its symbolic significance as a gateway for the Korean diaspora. item.title: Korean doctor operates remotely from Seoul on pig in Shanghai
item.description: Sitting at a console in Seoul, a Korean doctor successfully operated on a pig using a surgical robot about 870 kilometers away in Shanghai, marking Korea’s first cross-border telesurgery demonstration using a commercial platform. Kang Seok-ho, a professor of urology at Korea University College of Medicine, says the technology could profoundly transform surgical care, allowing doctors to operate from distant facilities and across borders, including on patients in disaster zones and battlefields. “I was delighted. I also found it remarkable that I could actually perform surgery in Shanghai from here,” Kang said in a recent interview with The Korea Times. The demonstration was conducted on Friday at Coex in Seoul during the Korean Urological Association’s annual meeting. The Toumai system developed by China’s MicroPort MedBot was used, according to the hospital. Telesurgery allows a physician to control surgical instruments through a communications network rather than being physically present in the same surgery as the patient. Unlike remote consultations, it involves the surgeon

item.title: Is AI investment slowing Naver's profits?
item.description: The outlook for internet giant Naver’s third-quarter earnings is turning gloomy, with analysts expecting operating profit to decline by double digits, citing spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and the slow monetization of AI services. According to market tracker FnGuide, the brokerage consensus estimate for Naver's third-quarter operating profit stood at 500 billion won ($377.5 million), down 12.4 percent from 570.66 billion won a year earlier, as of Wednesday. This contrasts with the projected 12 percent increase in revenue to 3.51 trillion won from 3.14 trillion won over the same period. Among the various factors, rising costs appear to be the biggest contributor to the decline. These include increased marketing expenses for Naver's commerce business, World Cup broadcasting rights costs reflected in the third-quarter results and higher depreciation expenses stemming from investments in graphics processing units (GPUs). item.title: Why has video of former presidential couple singing together surfaced now?
item.description: A video of former President Yoon Suk Yeol and his wife, Kim Keon Hee, singing a duet has been released, featuring the couple at the center of Korea’s first-ever case of a former president and first lady being detained simultaneously. The video was posted on social media by a close aide to Kim, prompting speculation that it may be intended to build public support for her release ahead of the expiration of her detention period at the end of this month. The video was posted Saturday by Jung Ji-won, a former administrative official at the presidential office who served as Kim’s aide during the Yoon administration. It shows the couple, dressed casually, singing “All I Ask of You” from the musical “The Phantom of the Opera” at what appears to be their residence. item.title: Capital soundness looms over major insurers' CEO reappointment decisions
item.description: With the terms of major insurers’ CEOs set to expire early next year, the companies’ capital strength is emerging as a key factor in their chances of reappointment, particularly as new rules requiring insurers to hold stronger financial cushion against losses are set to take effect in 2027, industry officials said Wednesday. The terms of Samsung Life Insurance CEO Hong Won-hak, Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance CEO Lee Mun-hwa, DB Insurance CEO Jeong Jong-pyo and Kyobo Life Insurance co-CEO Cho Dae-kyu are all due to expire in March. All four companies reported higher consolidated net profit in the first half of this year. Samsung Life posted 1.97 trillion won, followed by Samsung Fire & Marine with 1.37 trillion won, DB Insurance with 979.6 billion won and Kyobo Life with 704.8 billion won. item.title: Solidigm's potential Nasdaq IPO: Can Korean regulators intervene?
item.description: Korean regulators are facing calls to block a potential Nasdaq listing of Solidigm, SK hynix's U.S.-based NAND flash memory subsidiary, amid concerns that the move could undermine protections for shareholders of its Korean parent company, industry officials said Wednesday. "President Lee Jae Myung should use every means at his disposal to stop the listing," said Rep. Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party. "If Solidigm goes public, its rising valuation and shareholder base could dilute SK hynix shareholders' indirect stake in the company." Solidigm is owned by AI Company, a U.S.-based entity controlled by SK hynix. Further up the ownership chain are SK Square and SK Group's holding company, SK Inc. The dispute underscores Korea's complex corporate ownership structures, long criticized by retail investors as a factor behind the "Korea discount." In July, Korea introduced rules to protect minority shareholders from unfavorable dual listings. Under the rules, companies seeking to list carved-out subsidiaries domestically must meet shareholder approval and protection require

item.description: Hyundai Mobis will focus on verifying the real-world applicability and commercial viability of locally developed automotive semiconductors this year, as the industry seeks to reduce reliance on overseas suppliers amid the shift toward software-defined vehicles (SDVs), the auto parts maker said Wednesday. The company identified 19 joint system semiconductor projects with Korean companies over the past year, with development underway on 13 chips. Nine of the 13 have designated target vehicle models, bringing the projects closer to real-world application. Hyundai Mobis unveiled the progress at its second Auto Semicon Korea forum in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province. Participation expanded to 53 companies and institutions this year, up from 27 last year, as collaboration widened to include software, chip design intellectual property, packaging, testing and functional safety. item.description: Korean customers will be able to use Apple's generative artificial intelligence (AI)-powered assistant soon, as the tech giant is set to support Korean on its Siri AI starting this month, industry sources said Wednesday. The latest service expansion comes after Apple made a beta launch of the new Siri in English in September. item.title: Almonty Korea donates $9,000 to rural high school in Gangwon Province
item.description: Almonty Korea Tungsten, which operates a tungsten mine in Gangwon Province, said Wednesday it has donated 12 million won ($9,000) to Sangdong High School, a small rural school that turned to baseball as a way to avoid closing. The company handed over the donation Tuesday at the school in Sangdong, a town in Yeongwol County. It is the fourth consecutive year the company has supported the school’s baseball team. The Korean company is a subsidiary of Almonty Industries, a tungsten producer listed on the Nasdaq. Its Sangdong mine, located in the same town, began active mining in December last year. Tungsten is a hard, heat-resistant metal used in industries from electronics to defense. Sangdong High School faced closure when its enrollment fell to just three students. In 2023, with help from the local community, it reinvented itself as a school specializing in baseball. The team has since made quick progress. item.title: Korea space agency joins int'l satellite alliance for global disaster relief
item.description: The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA) said Wednesday it has joined the board of the International Charter: Space and Major Disasters, a global partnership in which space agencies provide satellite images to countries hit by disasters. KASA joined during the charter’s 56th regular board meeting at Ochanomizu Sola City in Tokyo, which opened Monday and continues through Friday. The space agency will take part in setting the charter’s policies as a board member starting in 2027. The charter is a voluntary, nonbinding partnership set up by space agencies for humanitarian, nonprofit purposes. When a major disaster such as an earthquake, typhoon or heavy snowfall strikes, member agencies take images of the affected area with their satellites, provide them to the country hit by the disaster and help analyze the damage. It has 17 member agencies from countries including the United States, France, Japan, China and India, as well as the European Space Agency. item.title: High tech, universal access propel Seoul subway to top of global rankings
item.description: When international travelers step onto a Seoul subway train platform, they are often struck by the lack of trash on the floor, delayed trains or dead zones on their smartphones. That seamless efficiency has now earned the Korean capital top honors in two major international transit rankings. British lifestyle media outlet "Time Out" placed the Korean capital fifth in its 2026 global transit survey — up three spots from last year — with 91.1 percent of surveyed residents expressing satisfaction. Meanwhile, CNN featured Seoul in its roundup of the world's 18 best metro systems, highlighting its cleanliness, high safety standards and tech-forward amenities. Behind the global accolades lies decades of aggressive infrastructure investment, particularly in passenger safety, accessibility and digital convenience. A central cornerstone of the system's safety record is its universal platform screen door network. item.description: The top U.S. military commander in South Korea called Wednesday for conducting more spread-out combined exercises between the allies throughout the year, rather than relying on the current biannual drills, citing the need to better adapt to an evolving security environment. U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) Commander Gen. Xavier Brunson made the remarks during a dialogue session in Seoul, saying he met with the South's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) Chairman Gen. Jin Yong-sung earlier this week to discuss their next springtime drills. item.title: Shoppers turn to warehouse stores as grocery bills climb
item.description: For Kim Eun-young, a 42-year-old mother of two living in Seoul’s Gwangjin District, a monthly trip to Costco has become routine this year. She used to pick up what she needed at a nearby supermarket, but rising prices prompted her to change her shopping habits. She said buying groceries and household essentials in bulk seems more economical, at least for her family of four. “The bill is bigger each time, but buying in bulk works out cheaper for the same amount,” Kim said. “I mainly buy food we eat regularly and everyday household essentials, and divide the food into meal-sized portions for storage.” Kim’s changing habits reflect a growing appetite for warehouse shopping as consumers seek relief from high prices. According to market tracker WiseApp Retail, combined estimated card spending at Costco and Emart Traders totaled a record 1.45 trillion won ($1.09 billion) in September. The estimates are based on a sample of Korean consumers’ credit and debit card payments. They exclude cash and bank transfers and therefore differ from the retailers’ reported revenue. Warehouse ret

item.title: Hanwha-Anthropic exhibition explores AI, human values through art
item.description: An exhibition exploring questions of how artificial intelligence (AI) systems work and how they are aligned with human values will take place in Seoul beginning this week, organizers said Wednesday. Titled "AS_____AS POSSIBLE," the exhibition co-hosted by the Hanwha Foundation of Culture and U.S. firm Anthropic, builder of the AI platform Claude, will open at the Centre Pompidou Hanwha on Friday, according to the organizers. The exhibition features five Korean artists and teams — MinOhrichar, Inhwa Yeom, Ubac Studio, Kahee Jeong and Mirim Chu -- who used Claude for their commissioned works on display. The title of the exhibition comes from questions surrounding the purpose and realm of technologies, with the possibility of the blank in the title being filled with words such as accurate, understandable and aligned. The exhibition runs through Nov. 13.

item.title: Seoul Architecture Festival draws 40,000 visitors in extended monthlong run
item.description: The 18th Seoul Architecture Festival drew about 40,000 citizens and architects during its run, which was extended to about a month this year, the Seoul Metropolitan Government said Wednesday. The festival was held from Sept. 15 to Oct. 11 at the Seoul Hall of Urbanism & Architecture in central Seoul under the theme “Assembling Seoul: Discovering Seoul.” Last year’s two-week edition drew 19,505 visitors. Its centerpiece exhibition, created in collaboration with a photographer, placed photos of Seoul’s urban architecture throughout a maze-like space so that visitors could look at familiar city scenes in a new way. The festival’s director built the exhibition spaces from recycled wooden pallets to keep down costs and environmental impact. An exhibition of the 10 winners of the 44th Seoul Architecture Awards, the city’s annual prize for buildings, was led by the grand prize winner, the Seo-Seoul Museum of Art, designed by THE_SYSTEM LAB. item.title: US ambassador urges fair treatment for American firms in Korea
item.description: U.S. Ambassador to Korea Michelle Steel on Wednesday called on Seoul to ensure that American companies operating in Korea can compete on a level playing field, amid U.S. concerns over regulations affecting firms such as Coupang. "American companies in Korea deserve to compete on a level playing field, fairly and without discrimination," Steel said in her opening remarks at a special luncheon hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea (AMCHAM) in Seoul. The event also featured Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of U.S. Forces Korea (USFK). Coupang, a U.S.-listed e-commerce firm that is active primarily in Korea, disclosed a data breach affecting over 33.6 million customers late last year, leading to an investigation and sanctions. In response, 50 U.S. Republican politicians signed a letter accusing Seoul of “targeted and discriminatory actions” against American companies, citing the Coupang case. item.title: Songdo opens biomanufacturing training center for global workforce
item.description: A new biomanufacturing training facility opened in Songdo, Incheon, on Monday to train workers from low and middle-income countries in vaccine and biopharmaceutical production. Incheon Free Economic Zone (IFEZ) authorities said the Global Bio Campus training facility held an opening ceremony at Yonsei University’s International Campus in Incheon, attended by World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Health Minister Jeong Eun-kyeong and IFEZ Commissioner Kim Jong-cheol. The facility was established in Songdo as part of efforts launched after WHO designated Korea as a Global Training Hub for Biomanufacturing (GTH-B) in February 2022. The ceremony also reviewed progress on the global biomanufacturing workforce training initiative and the development of its training infrastructure. item.title: Digital technology brings Korea's architectural heritage to life
item.description: Korea’s ancient architecture is moving beyond the ruins, with digital technology offering new ways to preserve historic sites and bring them to life for modern audiences. The National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage will host an international symposium on digital documentation and use of architectural heritage Nov. 4 at the WesternLife Hotel in Iksan, North Jeolla Province. The event will examine how digital records of historic buildings can support preservation, reconstruction and public engagement, drawing on examples from Korea, France and China. The symposium will also explore how cultural heritage data is being used beyond academic research, including in video games and immersive media, as researchers seek new ways to connect audiences with historic sites. The program features a keynote address by Kang Hyun of the institute on preserving and using architectural heritage through digital technology, followed by five presentations. item.title: Rarely opened gate links 2 Seoul palaces for exclusive night tours
item.description: Visitors will be able to walk between Changdeok Palace and Changgyeong Palace in central Seoul at night next month through a gate that is normally closed to the public, as part of a ticketed night tour, the Korea Heritage Service said Wednesday. The tour, called “Donggwol Dongnak,” runs from Nov. 10-15. It is organized by the agency’s Royal Palaces and Tombs Center and the Korea Heritage Agency. The two palaces were together known as Donggwol, or the “Eastern Palaces,” during the Joseon Dynasty (1392-1910) because they stood east of Gyeongbok Palace, the main royal palace. The 110-minute program combines a guided tour of both palaces with free time to explore their rear gardens. Guides playing court painters from Dohwaseo, the Joseon-era royal bureau of painting, will lead participants through major halls of Changgyeong Palace and the rear garden of Changdeok Palace. Short plays about historical figures linked to each site will be staged at four stops along the route. item.title: Coastal coffee capital of Korea mixes beachside reading with 'text hip' trend
item.description: Korea's tourism authorities are combining two of the country's biggest cultural obsessions — coffee and reading — for a seaside getaway this week on the nation's eastern coast. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) are hosting "Sea 24 Hours: Book Trip," a five-day outdoor reading event at Anmok Beach in Gangneung, running through Sunday. The event taps into "text hip," a viral trend among young Koreans who view reading physical books as a stylish, aesthetic lifestyle statement rather than just a quiet hobby. It is paired with the annual Gangneung Coffee Festival, which draws roughly 300,000 visitors to a coastal city widely celebrated as Korea’s specialty coffee capital. Set against a pine grove stretching along the sandy shoreline, the initiative also aims to encourage travelers to slow down, encouraging festivalgoers to linger longer in the region through a relaxed blend of coastal views, local coffee, and literature. The book lounge, open daily from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., offers about 200 books in four themed sections: food, photography

item.title: Japanese tourists flock to Haman County for unique cultural experiences
item.description: “Metcha kirei!” The Japanese exclamation, which means "it's really beautiful," rang out at Mujinjeong Pavilion in Haman County, South Gyeongsang Province, as dusk settled on the evening of Oct. 15. When local residents set fire to around 3,000 nak-hwa sticks — made by wrapping oak charcoal powder in hanji, traditional Korean paper, and twisting it into long wicks — a torrent of vivid red sparks rained down over the pond. Reflected on the water, the sparks blurred the boundary between heaven and earth, creating a dreamlike atmosphere. Each time the suspended lines were shaken, cascades of sparks poured down. “I’ve never seen fireworks that fall downward rather than shoot up into the sky. They’re truly magical,” said Sato Mio, 44, who visited from Osaka, Japan. “I’m amazed by the ingenuity of Koreans in the past, who created such beautiful displays of fire.” Her travel companion, Suzuki Ren, 47, gave a thumbs-up. “I’ve visited Seoul and Busan many times, but this is my first time in Haman,” he said. “I’d definitely like to come back if I get the chance.” Th

item.title: Korean Air tests UAM operations on island routes off Incheon
item.description: Korean Air said Wednesday it has successfully tested urban air mobility (UAM) operations on island routes off Korea's west coast, marking a step toward expanding the technology beyond population centers. The carrier conducted the demonstration Tuesday using a surrogate aircraft in cooperation with KT Corp., Hyundai Motor and Hyundai Engineering & Construction near the western port city of Incheon. Korean Air used its in-house Air Control & Routing Orchestrated Skyway System (ACROSS) to manage flight operations and air traffic, testing the system's capabilities in an island environment. The airline plans to complete the first phase of Incheon's UAM control system project in December as part of its efforts to develop traffic management and flight operations systems for future air taxi services.

item.title: District in Seoul automates bulky waste disposal with one-shot AI app
item.description: A district in Seoul is turning to computer vision to overhaul one of the most tedious chores of urban living: getting rid of old furniture and discarded household appliances. Eunpyeong District in northwestern Seoul has launched a pilot program using an artificial intelligence (AI) mobile application that allows residents to arrange bulky waste disposal by snapping a single photograph. The service is the first of its kind to be deployed by a municipality in Korea. Around the world, forward-looking metropolitan centers are racing to integrate machine learning into municipal waste management. Cities like Singapore and Zurich have deployed AI-powered robotic sorters and smart sensors in public bins to optimize collection. However, automating the resident-facing reporting process through consumer computer vision remains a rare frontier in smart city innovation — placing the Seoul district at the forefront of AI-driven urban convenience. In Korea, disposing of large items requires reporting each piece to the local district office and paying a designated collection fee. Previously, Eunpyeon

item.title: TWICE's Jihyo leaves JYP after 21 years to launch own agency
item.description: Jihyo, a member of K-pop girl group TWICE, said Wednesday she has left JYP Entertainment to establish her own agency. In a handwritten letter posted on social media, Jihyo said she had ended her contract with JYP, where she had been for 21 years since childhood. "I have established Emithaus," she wrote. "Through this new home, I hope to freely explore even the possibilities within myself that I have yet to discover." The 29-year-old singer added, "I will approach every future choice and activity with greater care and a stronger sense of responsibility, as I step out of a familiar environment and continue my work in a new way." Jihyo plans to pursue her solo music career under the new agency while continuing activities with TWICE. JYP Entertainment, one of Korea's major K-pop agencies, had managed Jihyo since she joined the company as a trainee before TWICE's 2015 debut.

item.description: OSLO/KYIV/WASHINGTON — U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday after what a U.S. official called "constructive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway, as President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war. The U.S. official said Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which also involved the leaders of Norway and Finland and European and NATO representatives, and that participants made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging Russia. The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture. item.title: Gwanghui Road Festa launches Seoul's downtown 'Gourmet Silk Road'
item.description: From Mongolian lamb ribs to Uzbek shashlik and Russian Napoleon cake, a unique food festival in central Seoul’s Gwanghui-dong neighborhood will offer visitors a taste of five cultures on Saturday, aiming to transform the multicultural district into a prime destination for global cuisine. The 2026 Gwanghui Road Festa will run from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., taking place across the commercial alleyways near Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station, according to the Seoul Credit Guarantee Foundation’s Myeongdong Comprehensive Support Center. Organized with Jung District, the festival is part of Seoul’s local-brand development initiative, which aims to promote the Central Asian street in Gwanghui-dong as a commercial district where food and cultures converge. item.title: Korean heritage schools in Japan turn to parents for curriculum overhaul
item.description: When heritage language schools gather to refine their teaching strategies, the focus traditionally rests on textbooks, grammar drills and classroom educators. But at a recent weekend summit in Japan, a fresh voice took center stage in the effort to preserve Korean culture among the next generation: the parents. Responding to direct feedback from the local Korean diaspora, the Overseas Koreans Agency joined hands with the Kansai Association of Korean Language Schools to host an innovative three-day training workshop in Osaka on Friday and Saturday. For decades, weekend Korean schools across Japan have served as cultural anchors for "Zainichi" — ethnic Koreans who settled in Japan primarily during the colonial era, along with their descendants. Today, Japan's Ministry of Justice registers more than 400,000 ethnic Korean residents, with the total Zainichi community estimated at around 1 million when including naturalized citizens and those with Japanese nationality. As generations shift and multiethnic households grow, maintaining linguistic ties to their ancestral homeland presents new c

item.title: Appeals court reduces ex-special counsel's sentence to 6 years in bribery case
item.description: An appellate court on Wednesday reduced former special counsel Park Young-soo's sentence on bribery-related charges by one year to six years in prison. The Seoul High Court also fined Park 200 million won ($150,000) and ordered him to forfeit 200 million won after finding him guilty of accepting the same amount from a private developer for campaign funds in his bid for the head of the Korean Bar Association. The court acknowledged the transactional nature of the exchange, noting the developer had asked Park, who then served as Woori Bank's board chair, for the bank to join talks on a consortium for the Daejang-dong property project in Seongnam, south of Seoul. A lower court had sentenced Park to seven years in prison after convicting him of accepting 300 million won from the developer. The appellate court found him guilty of accepting only 200 million won, citing inconsistencies in the developer's testimony on the rest of the amount. item.title: Korea expands farm technology support for war-scarred South Sudan
item.description: Korean peacekeepers deployed under the United Nations Mission in South Sudan are leveraging advanced agricultural science to help improve food security in one of the country's most vulnerable regions. The initiative, led by Korea’s Rural Development Administration in partnership with the military’s Hanbit Unit, integrates high-yield crop technologies into civil-affairs operations to help local communities work toward long-term agricultural self-sufficiency. Rather than relying solely on short-term food aid, Korean agricultural experts are embedding field-tested farming techniques into military civil assistance, establishing a scalable model for military-led development assistance. South Sudan, which gained independence in 2011 following decades of conflict, continues to suffer from severe food insecurity compounded by seasonal flooding, internal instability and economic shocks. The ongoing crisis in neighboring Sudan has further strained local resources as more than 1.4 million refugees and returnees have poured across the border since 2023, swelling demand for basic staples in alre
